records.mutation: name pair-enumeration itself as the trap that hides the balanced candidate, and replace it with a one-value-at-a-time test that must pass several live readings simultaneously
records.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling with the incumbent scored 2/8. Every one of the 6 failures began by enumerating factor pairs of the given number, which locked them into the multiplicative reading; they then proved each pair contradictory and still reported a member of that same list, sometimes explicitly calling it a contradiction one line before committing. One ran to the token cap looping over the same pairs. Both successes reached the balanced split where the two unknowns coincide, a candidate the factor-pair list can never produce. The incumbent tells the student to intersect constraints across live readings but never warns that enumerating pairs is the very habit that collapses those readings, so I named that trap, replaced it with testing one private value against each reading's requirement, and demanded the balanced candidate explicitly.

records.mutation: replace the incumbent's spot-check/symmetry-axis clause with a generic-member rule (carry one symbolic representative, avoid hand-computing instances) plus a stay-polynomial squared-modulus directive
records.subagent_summary: 7 of 8 fresh rollouts were correct; the lone failure reached the correct simplified locus and center/radius by clean symbolic algebra, then destroyed itself hand-computing an individual instance: it inverted a reciprocal (mishandling 1/(-i*sqrt3)), got a point off its own circle, and burned all 38k tokens re-auditing an already-correct derivation and declaring the substitution broken, never committing a value. Fifteen rounds of tuning the recheck/spot-check language have not removed this loop, so I removed the encouragement to test explicit points at all: prefer one generic symbolic member so the case index cancels, keep everything polynomial by imposing squared-modulus conditions and rooting only at the end, and repair rather than restart. This also transfers as general anti-case-enumeration and exactness discipline.

records.mutation: add a reference-point discipline: name the pinned distinguished point and forbid swapping a corner for a center, and require a concrete test point instead of a distance-to-sides containment argument
records.subagent_summary: Six of eight rollouts scored, so the incumbent's two-sided wedge bound and trade test are working and are kept. Both failures shared one specific slip, not a budget problem: each silently replaced the pinned corner with the big square's center, then argued that every side sits distance 1 from that center while the small piece only reaches 0.5, concluding total containment and a too-small union. One even reached the right partial overlap first and then talked itself back into containment; the other never closed reasoning while oscillating on that same claim. So this revision adds a reference-point rule (name the distinguished point the condition pins, never trade a corner for a center, a bound measured from the wrong reference voids what follows) and demands one concrete test point rather than a distance-to-sides containment argument.

records.mutation: add a residual-degree audit (subtracting a line leaves the leading term, so degree stays d, never d-1), assert reuse is allowed unless forbidden, and swap the open-ended count audit for a shrunken-case check
records.subagent_summary: Fresh 8 rollouts with the incumbent scored 4/8, no truncations, so length is not binding. The four failures split cleanly: two subtracted the affine target, declared the residual one degree below the piece degree, and reported a product one factor short per piece; one asserted each called number needs its own distinct piece and answered the bare piece count; one applied the per-piece root cap to the entire pattern and answered the bare degree. All four successes used the shared-affine-target residual framing, so that stays. The revision adds a one-clause degree audit (subtracting a line cannot touch the leading term, so the residual keeps full degree d, never d-1), states outright that reuse is allowed unless forbidden, and replaces the open-ended use-every-number audit with a small-case check, which is cheaper and transfers to other extremal counts.

records.mutation: insert a look-for-pattern-invariant-symmetry-via-small-cases clause ahead of the general algebra, keeping the rest of the incumbent intact
records.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling reproduced train 7/8 exactly as in the last round, so train is effectively pinned and only transfer can move J. The one failure was not arithmetic: it did the algebra correctly, then mis-screened a candidate against the domain, kept only the branch that collapses the figure, and reported the collapse instead of suspecting its own screening. Nine prior rounds already attacked that screening step directly with ever more specific root-checking clauses, and every one lost heldout; the incumbent's terse version scores best. So instead of a tenth restatement I left the incumbent wording intact and added one genuinely new and broadly useful step: probe small concrete cases for a pattern, invariant, or symmetry before committing to long general algebra.

records.mutation: replace the vague first-vs-last mechanics clause with a forced disambiguation: write both readings of the asked slot, then eliminate one by tracing one concrete run before any counting
records.subagent_summary: Fresh sampling with the incumbent gave 1/8; all rollouts ended normally around 10-15k tokens, so length is not the bottleneck. The first part is largely solved (5/8 got it), and every loss came from the slot-naming part: six of eight priced it as 1/n or 3!/4! by asserting each item equally likely in every position, and each of those had first silently reworded the deepest slot as "whatever was moved last", the opposite of what stacking on top implies. The incumbent only tells the student to pin whether the slot is the first or last arrival, which it obeys by picking a reading without checking. The revision makes that step adversarial: state both readings, then eliminate one by tracing a single concrete run to the end before any counting begins.

records.mutation: add the weighted-combination lever (build weights that cancel every unwanted term to isolate the single requested unknown) and a label-vs-condition-index discipline that reframes an inconsistent miniature as a translation slip rather than grounds for doubting the statement
records.subagent_summary: All 8 fresh rollouts scored 0; 7 of 8 hit the token cap without landing anything. The incumbent's small-instance advice was followed, but it backfired: rollouts mis-transcribed the miniature (confusing the summation label with the quantity that changes from condition to condition), got a contradictory tiny system, then spent thousands of tokens re-litigating whether the stated problem was even consistent, or distrusted small cases entirely. The two that reached a value pattern-matched a two-entry table onto the wrong family. Small cases alone cannot carry this: the revision keeps the commit-early and confirm-by-substitution discipline but adds a real structural lever -- take a weighted sum of the given conditions with weights chosen so every unwanted term cancels -- and pins the transcription so an inconsistent miniature is repaired instead of triggering an unbounded consistency loop.

records.mutation: keep the train-safe opening, small-cases clause and exact-arithmetic clause verbatim; insert an untried structure-exploiting lever menu (substitution, factoring/completing the square, symmetric sums, telescoping, complementary counting) before the closing commit-and-check
records.subagent_summary: All 8 fresh rollouts again scored reward 1 with clean stops at 3.0-7.0k tokens, so train is saturated and every gain must come from transfer. Reading the rollouts, the student's whole solution is one divisibility+percent chain; it never exercises the small-cases or exact-fractions clauses, and its only real waste is repeatedly relitigating which divisor to pick. Prior rounds show removing the question-anchored opening always collapses train (0.25-0.5), and further divisibility, scope-labelling, output-form, arithmetic-reliability, uniqueness-forcing, backward-reasoning and representation-change tails all lost held-out ground. So I kept the whole incumbent intact and inserted the one untried family of advice: concrete algebraic levers that eliminate unknowns before grinding, which should help transfer problems that are algebraic rather than divisibility-flavoured.

records.mutation: ban the vague relation-survey opening (commit to one structured form on line one and test it against the data at once) and add a free-parameter release rule: a parameter that cancels from every requested quantity means the problem is finished
records.subagent_summary: Seven of eight fresh rollouts were correct; the six shortest recentered on line one, pinned the center from the sum of the two given values, and stopped. The single failure ignored the coefficient ban, opened with eight unknowns, then drifted through a speculative survey (inverses, ad-hoc reduced forms, repeated "this is too vague") and ran to the token cap while grinding a degree-nine expansion. A near-miss pattern in earlier evidence was the same stall ending in an under-determined panic, where a leftover leading coefficient looked like a missing equation. So the revision keeps the working centered core but adds two guards: commit to one structured form immediately and test it against the data rather than surveying relations, and treat a parameter that cancels from everything asked as free rather than a reason to keep hunting equations.

records.mutation: use the requested answer shape as a falsification test: a parameterized result cannot be constant, so constant small cases are mis-traced and must be repaired before fitting, and the formula must reproduce the smallest trusted case
records.subagent_summary: 3 of 8 rollouts were correct. Four failures exhausted the 16384-token budget; the one finisher among the rest reported an exponent one too low. The shared root cause is new evidence: traces produced the SAME constant value at the first two or three sizes, after which the student either fitted an off-by-one exponent to that table or looped for thousands of tokens arguing "this suggests a constant, but it must be an expression in the parameter, so it is more complex". One dead rollout also built a map sending four inputs to one output and theorized about it instead of redoing the trace. The revision therefore turns the requested answer shape into a falsification test: a parameterized result cannot be constant, so constant small cases are mis-traced and must be repaired before any formula is fitted, the formula must reproduce the smallest trusted case, a non-injective hand map is a slip, and a fitting value is stated at once.
